market_context: United States; aged and fresh dairy cheese in the context of lactose intolerance
title: Why do some cheeses contain so little lactose?

seo.title: Why do some cheeses contain so little lactose?
seo.meta_description: Cheesemaking removes much of milk’s lactose with the whey, and starter bacteria ferment most of what remains. That is why many hard aged cheeses contain far less lactose than milk.
seo.search_intent: Explain how whey drainage and fermentation reduce lactose in cheese and what that means for lactose intolerance.

excerpt: Cheese is made from milk, but it does not keep all of milk’s lactose. Roughly 98% of milk lactose is removed in whey or converted to lactic acid during cheesemaking, and residual lactose is metabolized early in ripening. Many firm aged cheeses therefore end up with very small amounts.
content_html:
A slice of aged cheese can be made from lactose-containing milk and still have very little lactose left. The reason is that cheesemaking is a separation and fermentation process, not just a way of turning liquid milk solid.

Most lactose follows the whey

Lactose is dissolved in milk’s watery phase. When casein coagulates into curd, much of that water drains away as whey. A major review of cheese biochemistry estimates that about 98% of the lactose in milk is removed in whey or converted to lactic acid during manufacture.

Starter cultures consume the remainder

Cheese cultures use lactose for energy and make lactic acid. Residual lactose in the curd drops rapidly during the early stages of ripening. In a well-aged hard cheese, that leaves very little milk sugar compared with the original milk.

The difference from milk can be large

NIDDK notes that a 1.5-ounce serving of low-fat hard cheese can contain less than 1 gram of lactose, compared with roughly 11 to 13 grams in 1 cup of low-fat milk.

Those values are not labels for every cheese, but they explain why many people with lactose intolerance find Cheddar, Swiss and other hard cheeses easier to tolerate than a glass of milk.

Does older always mean lower lactose?

Aging often pushes lactose lower, but age alone is not a perfect predictor. Whey drainage, moisture, starter culture, acidity and the individual production method all matter. Fresh high-moisture cheeses can retain more lactose; pressed aged cheeses generally lose more watery whey and undergo more fermentation.

Low lactose is not dairy-free

Lactose intolerance involves digestion of the milk sugar lactose. Milk allergy involves milk proteins and the immune system. An aged cheese with almost no lactose still contains dairy proteins, so “low lactose” is not a safety claim for a milk allergy.

How can you know the amount in one cheese?

You cannot calculate it precisely just from hardness or age. If you need a very strict limit, look for a lactose-free claim or manufacturer testing. If you have ordinary lactose intolerance, your own dose tolerance matters too; NIDDK notes that many people can tolerate some lactose without symptoms.

The useful mental model

Think of lactose reduction in two stages: drain it out with whey, then ferment what remains. Aging is the continuation of a process that began in the vat.

faq.question: Is aged cheese lactose-free?
faq.answer: Many aged cheeses have very little lactose, but you should not assume zero unless the product is tested or labeled accordingly.

faq.question: Why is hard cheese lower in lactose than milk?
faq.answer: Much of the lactose leaves with whey, and starter bacteria ferment residual lactose into lactic acid.

faq.question: Is low-lactose cheese safe for a milk allergy?
faq.answer: No. It still contains milk proteins. Lactose intolerance and milk allergy are different conditions.
